subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Status Quo Bias
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Status Quo Bias.

hook.text: Most organ donation rates depend on the default option on a form, not on how people feel about donation.

buildup.text: Status quo bias is the preference for keeping things as they are. Change requires effort; staying put is free.

discovery.text: Samuelson and Zeckhauser showed people stick with defaults even when alternatives are clearly better.

twist.text: Companies exploit this with auto-renewals. The default keeps customers paying even when they want to leave.

climax.text: Review your defaults annually: subscriptions, investments, routines. Ask if you would choose them today from scratch.

punchline.text: The default is a decision someone else made for you.

quiz.question: What drives high organ donation rates in some countries?
options: The default option on the form is opt-in
People feel strongly about saving lives

details.summary: Status quo bias is the preference for the current state of affairs where any change is perceived as a loss. People stick with existing products, investments, jobs, and arrangements even when better alternatives are available because switching feels risky.
details.whyItMatters: Status quo bias costs individuals and organizations enormous amounts by preventing beneficial changes, upgrades, and adaptations. The psychological comfort of the familiar outweighs the rational benefits of improvement.
takeaways: People prefer existing situations even when objectively better alternatives exist
Change is framed as loss, making the current state feel more valuable than it is
Defaults harness status quo bias by making a specific option the starting point

faq.question: Why is the status quo so psychologically powerful?
faq.answer: Loss aversion makes potential losses from changing loom larger than potential gains. The known current situation has the advantage of familiarity. Uncertainty about alternatives triggers risk aversion. All three mechanisms favor staying put.

faq.question: How can organizations overcome status quo bias?
faq.answer: Frame the status quo as also a choice with costs and risks, not as a safe default. Make the cost of inaction explicit. Require periodic re-justification of existing approaches rather than only requiring justification for changes.
